title: Braking and regeneration
goals: Say when a motor on a drive becomes a generator, and where the energy goes
Work out the energy in a spinning load and the braking power to stop it in a given time
Choose between a longer ramp, DC injection, a brake resistor, a regenerative drive and a mechanical brake
Size a brake resistor's average and peak power
Explain a DC bus overvoltage trip on deceleration, and cure it
summary:
A motor is also a generator. When the load drives the motor faster than the drive is asking for (slowing a heavy flywheel, lowering a hoist, an unwinder) the energy flows **back into the drive**.

A standard drive rectifies the mains into a **DC bus**: about $\sqrt{2} \times 400 \approx 565$ V on a 400 V supply. Its diode rectifier cannot send energy back to the mains, so returning energy **charges the bus capacitors**, the bus voltage rises, and at a limit (typically around 800 V on a 400 V drive: check its manual) the drive trips on **DC bus overvoltage**.

Energy in a spinning load: $E = \tfrac{1}{2}J\omega^2$, with $J$ the inertia (kg·m²) and $\omega = \frac{2\pi n}{60}$ (rad/s). Stopping it in time $t$ at a steady rate takes an average power $\frac{E}{t}$, and twice that at the start (power = torque × speed, and the speed falls to zero).

The choices:

- **Longer deceleration ramp**: the motor's and drive's own losses soak it up. Free. Many drives have an **overvoltage controller** that stretches the ramp automatically.
- **DC injection** (or flux braking): DC in the stator brakes the motor and turns the energy into heat **in the motor**. For stopping, not for frequent heavy braking.
- **Brake chopper and resistor**: the drive switches the bus onto a resistor when the bus rises; the energy becomes heat in the resistor.
- **Regenerative (active front end) drive** or a **common DC bus** shared with motoring drives: the energy is used, not burnt.
- **Mechanical brake**: for holding at standstill and for emergencies, not for routine stopping on a drive.

**Resistor sizing**: its resistance must not be below the drive's minimum (the chopper's current limit); its **peak** power is about $\frac{V^2}{R}$ at the chopper's switch-on voltage; its **average** power is the energy per cycle ÷ the cycle time.

formulas.name: Kinetic energy of a spinning load
formulas.says: A spinning load stores energy that grows with its inertia and with the square of its speed.

formulas.name: rpm to rad/s
formulas.says: One turn is 2π radians; n turns a minute is n ÷ 60 a second.

formulas.name: DC bus voltage
formulas.says: The rectifier charges the bus to about the peak of the line voltage.
formulas.example: 400 V supply: about 565 V on the bus (a little less under load).

formulas.name: Resistor peak power
formulas.says: When the chopper switches the bus onto the resistor, the power is the bus voltage squared over the resistance.
symbols: the bus voltage when the chopper is on (V)

bench.task: Look at a drive at work that stops a big load (a fan, a flywheel, a hoist) and find out how it handles the energy. Read only: the drive's parameters and its documentation.
check: Find the deceleration ramp time and whether the overvoltage controller is on
Look for a brake resistor (often on top of the cabinet, with a thermal switch) or a regenerative unit
Check the fault log for any DC overvoltage trips
Estimate the load's energy at full speed and the average power over the ramp

cards.q: A drive stops a large fan in 5 seconds. It trips on 'DC overvoltage' every time it stops, but never while running. Why?
options: The fan's energy is coming back faster than the drive can lose it
The mains voltage rises whenever the fan slows
The acceleration ramp is too short for the fan
The fan's motor is too small for the drive
cards.why: Slowing the fan quickly turns the motor into a generator. The energy goes into the drive's DC bus, which cannot pass it back to the mains, so the bus voltage rises until the drive trips. A longer ramp, or a brake resistor, cures it. A short acceleration ramp gives overcurrent, not overvoltage.

cards.title: When the motor becomes a generator
cards.body:
An induction motor runs a little **slower** than the drive's field (slip) when it is driving the load. If the load drives the motor **faster** than the field, the slip reverses and the motor **generates**: energy flows back to the drive.

That happens when:

- the drive **slows** a load with a lot of inertia faster than friction would
- an **overhauling** load pushes it: lowering a hoist, a conveyor running downhill
- an **unwinder** is held back to keep the web in tension
cards.more:
A car going downhill in a low gear: the engine holds it back, and the wheels drive the engine. That is engine braking.

On a drive, the drive lowers its output frequency to slow down. If the load's inertia keeps the motor spinning faster than that new frequency, the rotor overtakes the field, and the motor turns the load's kinetic energy into electrical energy.

A fan coasting to a stop gives nothing back. Ask it to stop faster than it would coast, and the drive must take that energy somewhere.

cards.q: Which of these regenerates energy into the drive?
options: Lowering a load on a hoist at steady speed
Raising a load on a hoist at steady speed
A pump running at a steady speed
A conveyor speeding up to its working speed
cards.why: Lowering, gravity drives the load down and the motor holds it back: it generates the whole time. Raising, accelerating, and steady pumping all take energy from the drive.

cards.title: Where it goes: the DC bus
cards.body:
A standard drive **rectifies** the mains with diodes into a **DC bus**, smoothed by big capacitors: about $\sqrt{2}$ times the line voltage, so about **565 V** on a 400 V supply.

Diodes only pass energy **in**. Energy coming back from the motor **charges the capacitors**, and the bus voltage climbs. At a limit (typically around **800 V** for a 400 V drive) the drive **trips on DC overvoltage** to protect its parts. The motor then coasts.
cards.more:
Think of the bus as a water tank filled from the mains through non-return valves. Normally the motor draws from it. When the motor generates, it pours water back in, and the valves stop it going back to the mains. The level rises until an overflow alarm trips.

Numbers: $\sqrt{2} \times 400 = 566$ V with no load; a little less while running (about 540 V). The capacitors can absorb only a small amount before reaching the trip level, about the energy of the last second of a small fan's stop.

Before working inside a drive, the bus must be **discharged**: wait the time on the label (often 5 minutes or more) and **measure** it, because the capacitors hold lethal energy after the supply is off.

cards.q: A drive runs from a {vll} V three-phase supply. Roughly what is its DC bus voltage, with no load?
cards.why: The rectifier charges the capacitors to the peak of the line-to-line voltage: about 1.41 times the RMS value. Under load it sags to about 1.35 times.
cards.hint: The bus charges to the peak of the line voltage.

cards.title: How much energy is spinning
cards.body:
A spinning load holds energy:

$$E = \tfrac{1}{2}J\omega^2$$

$J$ is its **inertia** in kg·m² (how hard it is to spin up), $\omega$ (omega) its speed in **radians per second**: $\omega = \frac{2\pi n}{60}$ from rpm.

The energy goes with speed **squared**: twice the speed, four times the energy.

Stop it in a time $t$ at a steady rate and the **average** braking power is $\frac{E}{t}$; at the start of the stop it is about **twice** that.
cards.more:
A radian is the angle where the arc equals the radius; there are $2\pi$ (about 6.28) in a turn. So 1500 rpm is $1500 \times 6.28 \div 60 = 157$ rad/s.

A 2 kg·m² flywheel at 1500 rpm: $0.5 \times 2 \times 157^2 = 24\,700$ J, 24.7 kJ. Stopped in 5 s: 4.9 kW on average.

Why twice at the start? Braking power is torque times speed. A steady ramp uses a steady braking torque, while the speed falls from full to zero, so the power falls in a straight line from its peak to nothing. The average of a straight line from a peak to zero is half the peak.

cards.q: A load of inertia {j} kg·m² spins at {n} rpm. How much kinetic energy does it hold, in kJ?
cards.why: Speed into rad/s first; then half J ω². Using rpm straight in the formula gives a number about 90 times too big.

cards.title: Five ways to deal with it
cards.body:
- **Longer ramp**: give it more time; the motor's and drive's losses absorb a slow stop. Many drives' **overvoltage controller** stretches the ramp automatically.
- **DC injection** (or **flux braking**): makes the **motor** turn the energy into heat. Good for stopping now and then, not for heavy, frequent braking.
- **Brake chopper and resistor**: a transistor switches the bus onto a resistor whenever the bus voltage rises; the resistor gets hot.
- **Regenerative drive** (active front end), or a **common DC bus** with drives that are motoring: the energy is reused.
- **Mechanical brake**: holds at standstill and stops in an emergency; not for routine stops.
cards.more:
Pick by how much energy and how often.

A fan that stops twice a day: a longer ramp, or let it coast. A centrifuge that must stop in 20 s every few minutes: a brake resistor. A crane hoist lowering all day, or a test rig: a regenerative drive pays for itself in energy.

DC injection puts direct current through the stator, making a stationary field that drags the rotor to a stop. All the energy ends up as heat in the rotor, so the motor heats up; it is fine for an occasional quick stop or for holding a fan still before starting it.

On a hoist, the mechanical brake holds the load; the drive does the lowering and the stopping, and the brake is applied once the motor is at standstill.

cards.q: Match each job with the braking method that suits it best.
pairs: A fan that may take a minute to stop
A centrifuge stopped quickly every few minutes
A hoist that lowers loads all day
Holding a lift car at a floor
cards.why: Little energy: a ramp. Frequent bursts: a resistor. Continuous regeneration: give it back. Holding at standstill: a mechanical brake.

cards.title: Sizing a brake resistor
cards.body:
Three numbers:

- **Resistance**: not **below** the drive's minimum (set by the chopper's current limit). Lower resistance draws more current.
- **Peak power**: when the chopper is on, $P = \frac{V^2}{R}$, with $V$ the bus voltage at which it switches (often about 750–800 V on a 400 V drive).
- **Average power**: the energy dumped per cycle ÷ the time of one cycle. The resistor's continuous rating must cover this.

The resistor gets very hot: mount it where it can cool, and wire its **thermal switch** into the drive's run enable.
cards.more:
Numbers: a 60 Ω resistor and a chopper at 780 V. Peak: $780^2 \div 60 = 10\,140$ W, about 10 kW while braking hardest.

Each cycle dumps 25 kJ, and a cycle takes 60 s: $25\,000 \div 60 = 417$ W on average. So a resistor rated about 500 W continuous, able to take 10 kW peaks, will do (the manufacturer's tables pair drives with resistors).

The thermal switch matters: if the chopper fails shorted, the resistor sits across the bus permanently and will overheat. The switch opens, the drive stops, and nothing catches fire.

cards.q: A brake chopper switches on at {v} V. The resistor is {r} Ω. What is the peak power in the resistor?
cards.why: While the chopper is on, the whole bus voltage is across the resistor: $P = \frac{V^2}{R}$.

cards.q: A flywheel of 2 kg·m² runs at 1500 rpm and must stop in 5 s, every 30 s. What braking energy, average power during the stop, peak power, and average resistor power over the cycle?

steps.ask: Peak power, at the start of the stop.

steps.show: $24\,700 \div 30 = 820$ W (ignoring the motor's and drive's losses, which help)

cards.why: Energy from inertia and speed; power from energy and time. The resistor's peak rating comes from the stop; its continuous rating from the whole cycle.

cards.q: Why is the peak braking power about twice the average in step 4?
cards.context: Average 4.9 kW over the 5 s stop; peak 9.9 kW.
cards.model: Braking power is torque times speed. A steady ramp needs a steady braking torque, but the speed falls from full to zero over the stop. So the power starts at its highest (full torque at full speed) and falls in a straight line to zero. The average of a straight line falling from a peak to zero is half the peak, so the peak is twice the average.
points: Speed falls to zero, so power does too
Average of a straight-line fall is half the peak

cards.q: The same flywheel (24.7 kJ at 1500 rpm). The drive and motor can absorb about 2 kW on their own. How long a ramp avoids needing a resistor?

steps.ask: The peak power must stay under 2 kW. The peak is twice the average, so the average must be under…
Time to spread 24.7 kJ at 1 kW on average.

steps.show: About 25 s or longer (or let the overvoltage controller stretch it)

cards.why: Turn the sums round: allowed power gives the time. If the process cannot wait 25 s, fit a resistor.

cards.q: A load holds {e} kJ at full speed. The drive can absorb a peak of {p} kW without a resistor. What is the shortest steady ramp to standstill?
cards.why: The peak is twice the average, so the average must be half the allowed peak; time = energy ÷ average power.
cards.hint: Average power = peak ÷ 2; time = energy ÷ average power.

cards.q: Each machine cycle dumps {e} kJ into a brake resistor, and a cycle lasts {t} s. What average power must the resistor take?
cards.why: Average power = energy ÷ time, over the whole cycle. Its peak rating must also cover the hardest moment of the stop.
cards.hint: Energy in joules ÷ the cycle time.

cards.q: Working out a 0.5 kg·m² drum's energy at 1200 rpm. One line is wrong. Which?
lines: So 360 kJ to get rid of
cards.why: The formula needs rad/s, not rpm. rpm × 2π ÷ 60 is about rpm ÷ 9.55, and squaring makes the slip about 90 times too big.

cards.q: DC injection braking is used to stop a saw blade quickly. Where does the blade's energy end up?
options: As heat in the motor
Back in the mains supply
In the drive's DC bus capacitors
In a brake resistor
cards.why: DC in the stator makes a stationary field; the spinning rotor is dragged to a stop and its energy becomes heat in the motor. That is why DC injection suits occasional stops, not heavy, frequent braking.

cards.q: On a hoist driven by a VFD, when should the mechanical brake be applied in a normal stop?
options: Once the drive has brought it to standstill
At the start of the deceleration ramp
Whenever the load is moving downwards
Never: the drive alone holds the load
cards.why: The drive does the stopping and holds the load at zero speed; the brake then closes to hold it, and the drive stops. Braking a moving load on the brake wears it fast and fights the drive. In an emergency the brake closes at once.

cards.q: A loaded conveyor of {m} kg (belt, load and all moving parts, as an equivalent mass) moves at {v} m/s. How much kinetic energy must be removed to stop it, in kJ?
cards.why: Straight-line motion uses $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$, the twin of $\tfrac{1}{2}J\omega^2$. Conveyors usually hold little energy for their size: friction stops them quickly anyway.

cards.q: Match each trip with what usually causes it.
pairs: Acceleration ramp too short for the inertia
Deceleration ramp too short, no resistor
DC overvoltage while lowering a hoist
Continuous regeneration, resistor missing or failed
A supply dip or a lost phase
cards.why: Speeding up draws current; slowing down pushes energy back and raises the bus voltage.

cards.q: A load holds {e} kJ at {n1} rpm. How much does it hold at {n2} rpm?
cards.why: Energy goes with speed squared: half the speed, a quarter of the energy; double, four times.
cards.hint: What power of the speed is in $\tfrac{1}{2}J\omega^2$?

cards.q: Why does a fan usually need no brake resistor, even with a fairly short ramp?
options: Air resistance slows it hard, soaking up its energy
Fans have almost no inertia
Fans cannot regenerate at all
The affinity laws stop energy coming back
cards.why: A fan's load torque rises with speed squared, so air friction does much of the braking at high speed. Big fans do have inertia, though: if the ramp is shorter than the fan would coast down in, it will still regenerate.

cards.q: A centrifuge trips on DC overvoltage when it is stopped. Which change cures it without slowing the process?
options: Fit a brake chopper and resistor
Shorten the deceleration ramp
Lengthen the acceleration ramp
Raise the drive's current limit
cards.why: The energy must go somewhere: a resistor takes it as heat while keeping the stop quick. A longer ramp would also cure it, but slows the process.

cards.q: {j} kg·m² at {n} rpm. Kinetic energy in kJ?
cards.why: rpm to rad/s, then half J ω².

cards.q: {e} kJ removed in a {t} s stop. Average braking power, in kW?
cards.why: Energy ÷ time. The peak is about twice this.
